title: This Flash Travelled 10 Billion Years to Reach Earth
paragraphs: On the fourth of March, twenty twenty-four, a radio telescope in South Africa caught a flash. It lasted only a few thousandths of a second. But that flash had been travelling for more than ten billion years.
It left its home when the universe was only about three billion years old. Before the Sun existed. Before the Earth existed.
Astronomers call it a fast radio burst. This one is the most distant ever traced back to its home galaxy. It more than doubles the previous record.
Its name is F R B twenty twenty-four oh three oh four B. And the galaxy it came from was so faint that the biggest telescopes on the ground saw nothing at all.
So what makes a flash this powerful, and what happened to it on a journey of ten billion years?

Let's start with the flash itself. A fast radio burst is a sudden blast of radio waves from deep space. Radio waves are a kind of light, just with waves far too long for our eyes to see. Most last just a few milliseconds. The first one was reported in two thousand seven.
What causes them is still not settled. Theorists have come up with nearly one hundred ideas to explain them. And they arrive at random, from any direction in the sky.
This one was strong, even for a fast radio burst. The research team estimates its energy at around ten to the forty-one ergs. That is roughly as much energy as our Sun gives off in many months.
All of it released in a few thousandths of a second. Shorter than a single blink.
Here's the part I find most striking. Nobody can see the object that made this flash. Everything we know about it comes from two clues: the flash itself, and the galaxy around it.
So what could release that much energy, that fast? One of the leading suspects is a magnetar.

When a very massive star runs out of fuel, it explodes as a supernova. Its core can collapse into a neutron star, a ball of matter so dense that it squeezes more than the mass of the Sun into something about the size of a city. A magnetar is a young neutron star with an extreme magnetic field.

Magnetars have the strongest magnetic fields known anywhere in the universe. One idea is that when that field suddenly snaps and rearranges, it releases a burst of energy. That is one of the ways a single object could produce a flash this bright.
The team's data point toward a young magnetar here. They also tested another idea, a collision between two neutron stars. Lead researcher Manisha Caleb says that is very unlikely for this burst.
But one of her co-authors, Xavier Prochaska, puts it carefully. As he says, observers like him can only kill models, never prove them. So the magnetar is the best suspect, not a closed case.
Now follow the flash. It leaves its galaxy when the universe is about three billion years old. Ahead of it lies about eighty percent of all cosmic history.

For billions of years, it crosses empty space. Galaxies form and merge around its path. Stars are born and die by the billions. And the whole universe keeps expanding, stretching the waves as they travel.
More than five billion years into the trip, a cloud of gas in an ordinary galaxy collapses. It becomes our Sun. Then the Earth forms around it.
The flash keeps going. Life appears on Earth. The dinosaurs rise and disappear. Humans build the first radio telescopes.
And the flash is still on its way.

It is also not travelling through a perfect vacuum. Between the galaxies there is a thin fog of gas, too faint to see. As the burst passes through, that gas slows the lower radio frequencies more than the higher ones.
So the flash arrives smeared out. The high notes come first, and the low notes trail behind. How long that delay is tells astronomers how much gas the burst crossed on the way.

Near the end of its trip, this burst passes close to the Virgo Cluster, a giant crowd of galaxies. Then through the gas around our own Milky Way. And then, on the fourth of March, twenty twenty-four, it reaches Earth.

What caught it was MeerKAT, a radio telescope made of sixty-four dishes in South Africa. It was running an ordinary observation that night. A system called MeerTRAP watches the data in real time for exactly this kind of flash.
Because MeerKAT uses many dishes working together, it can pin down where a burst came from very precisely. That point on the sky was the address. Now astronomers needed to see the house.

They pointed some of the largest telescopes on the ground at that spot. One of them was Keck, in Hawaii, with a mirror ten metres across. They looked in visible light and in near infrared. Prochaska's verdict was simple. [sigh] There was simply nothing to see.
That's where the James Webb Space Telescope came in. Webb sees in infrared, and it is built to catch faint light from the early universe. And at that exact spot, it found a galaxy.

This is where the flash was born. And it surprised the team. In the words of co-author Laura Driessen, the galaxy is surprisingly small, metal-poor, and undergoing a very active episode of star formation.

Small means it is a dwarf galaxy, a tiny fraction of the size of our Milky Way. Metal-poor means it is made mostly of the simplest elements, hydrogen and helium. And very active means it is building new stars quickly.
Where many stars are being born, the biggest ones die young. They explode, and some of them leave behind newborn magnetars. That is why this little galaxy fits the magnetar idea so well.

Here's what I think is the real lesson. A galaxy too faint for the biggest telescopes on the ground was found because a flash a few milliseconds long pointed straight at it. The burst wasn't just the discovery. It was the flashlight.

And the flashlight lights up more than its own galaxy. For a long time, astronomers couldn't find a large share of the ordinary matter that should be in the universe. Much of it is hiding as that thin gas between the galaxies.
Fast radio bursts are one of the few ways to measure it. Every burst that crosses the gap records how much gas it passed through. Astronomers say that lets them, in effect, weigh the universe.

Most of the bursts with known home galaxies come from much closer to us. This one crossed about eighty percent of cosmic history. That makes it one of the deepest single measurements of that hidden gas so far.

The results were published in the journal Science in October twenty twenty-six. And bigger telescopes are coming. MeerKAT is a forerunner of the Square Kilometre Array, now being built in South Africa and Australia.

Here's the part I keep coming back to. The flash travelled for more than ten billion years. It arrived during an ordinary night of observing, and it was over in milliseconds. Catching it took the right dishes, the right software, and a space telescope to finish the job.
A few thousandths of a second of radio waves. More than ten billion years on the road. Older than the Sun, older than the Earth, and it still told us where it came from.
So here's a question for you. What do you think made it: a magnetar, or something nobody has thought of yet? Tell me in the comments.
